status: DRAFT v0.1: not yet reviewed, pretested or calibrated.
notes: Federalism views often follow which party holds federal power. Items ask for rules 'under any administration' and the states_differ item spans issues favored by both sides, so a consistent federalist can be told apart from someone who wants their side's policy at whatever level wins. High pole is consistently 'more state and local control'.

items.subtopic: Federal vs state power in general
items.stem: Which comes closer to your view?
items.scope: Think about major policies in general, whichever party is in power.

sides.label: National standards
sides.text: Major policies should be set nationally, so rules are the same everywhere, even if some states disagree.

sides.label: State control
sides.text: States should decide most policies, even if rules differ from state to state.

items.subtopic: Federal vs state power in general
items.stem: Which comes closer to your view of who solves problems better?
items.scope: Problems like roads, schools and public health.

sides.label: Federal government
sides.text: The federal government, which has more money and expertise, even if it is far from local conditions.

sides.label: State and local
sides.text: State and local governments, which are closer to people, even if some lack money or expertise.

items.subtopic: Letting states differ on contested issues
items.stem: For each of these, should the rules be the same nationwide, or decided by each state?
items.scope: Answer each one separately. This is about who decides, not what the rule should be.

cases.text: Voting rules, such as mail voting and voter ID

items.stem: Should state governments be able to stop cities from passing their own laws on things like minimum wage, guns or plastic bags?
items.scope: Answer whichever party controls your state or your city.
options: Only where one statewide rule is clearly needed
No; cities should set their own rules

items.stem: Should the federal government be able to withhold money from states that don't follow its policies?
items.scope: Answer for any administration, and policies you like or dislike.
options: Yes, on any policy it chooses
Only for conditions about how that money is spent
No conditions; give states the money to spend as they see fit

items.stem: Should the federal government be able to cut funding to states or cities for each of these reasons?
items.scope: Answer each case separately, under any administration.

cases.text: Refusing to help with federal immigration enforcement
Letting transgender girls play on girls' school teams
Banning transgender girls from girls' school teams

items.notes: Mirror cases: the same rule with each side benefiting. Consistency across cases is scored separately (preregistration §6a).

items.stem: Should states be able to refuse to help enforce federal laws they disagree with?
items.scope: Think about federal laws in general, under any administration. Specific laws come next.
options: No; states must help with federal enforcement
States can decline to use their own police and resources, but not block federal agents
States can refuse and pass laws blocking enforcement within their borders

items.stem: Should a state be able to refuse to help enforce each of these federal laws?
items.notes: Mirror cases: the same rule with each side benefiting. Consistency across cases is scored separately (preregistration §6a).

items.stem: Overall, how big should the federal government be?
items.scope: Think about what it does and spends, not about any particular administration.

items.stem: When it's unclear which policy works best, which approach is closer to your view?
items.scope: Policies on things like health care, schools or welfare.

sides.label: One national approach
sides.text: Pick one national approach based on the best evidence, even if states can't try alternatives.

sides.label: Let states experiment
sides.text: Let states try different approaches, even if some get it wrong and people there are worse off.
